subject: ENG
title: Kaveri
status: DRAFT — for review by an English teacher before any question is approved
source: Written against NCERT Class IX English ‘Kaveri’ (iebe1, the new NCERT book), read from the chapter PDFs, to the CBSE English Language and Literature (184) question paper design: extracts, short answers and long answers. The CBSE 2025-26 syllabus still names Beehive and Moments; these follow Kaveri, as the curriculum drafts do. Extracts are checked word for word by scripts/check-english-questions.mjs.

questions.stem: On the moonlit terrace, the grandmother tells her twelve-year-old granddaughter the story of her own life — losing her mother, never going to school, marrying young. What was she most likely leading up to?

options.text: Asking her granddaughter to help her learn to read.
Complaining that her father had married again.
Persuading her granddaughter to take her to Kashi.
Scolding her granddaughter for staying away for a week.

questions.explanation: The narrator senses 'there had to be some reason why she was talking to me'. The story of a girlhood without school leads straight to 'Yes, I need your help' and her decision to learn the Kannada alphabet.

questions.stem: Why was the grandmother, more than anybody else, eager to know what happened next in Kashi Yatre?

options.text: She knew Triveni, the writer of the novel.
Like the old lady in the novel, she had never gone to Kashi, and identified with her.
She had given away her savings for an orphan girl's wedding.
Her friends at the temple had already read the ending to her.

questions.explanation: 'My grandmother too never went to Kashi, and she identified herself with the novel's protagonist. So more than anybody else she was the one most interested in knowing what happened next in the story.'

questions.stem: When her grandmother touched her feet, the narrator was 'surprised and taken aback'. Here 'taken aback' means

options.text: offended by a lack of respect
embarrassed in front of others
surprised by something unexpected
pleased by an unusual gift

questions.explanation: The lesson glosses 'taken aback' as 'surprised by something unexpected'. Elders never touch the feet of youngsters, so the narrator did not expect it.

questions.stem: 'Hide and seek' is a binomial — two words used together in a fixed order. Which binomial from the lesson's list means 'succeed or fail without help'?

options.text: part and parcel
sooner or later
pick and choose
sink or swim

questions.explanation: 'Sink or swim' means to succeed or fail without help. 'Part and parcel' means belonging to something, 'sooner or later' means at some time in the future, and 'pick and choose' means choosing only the best.

questions.stem: In 'Bharat Our Land', the line 'she's peerless, let's praise her!' closes both stanzas. What is the main effect of repeating it?

options.text: It marks a shift from praising India to questioning it.
It shows the poet is unsure whether India has an equal.
It invites readers to join the poet in celebrating a land without equal.
It contrasts India's glorious past with a weaker present.

questions.explanation: 'Peerless' means without an equal, and 'let's praise her' draws the reader in. Repeated as a refrain, it reinforces the poet's pride and his call to celebrate India; nothing in the poem doubts or criticises the land.

questions.extract: ‘Yes, I need your help. You know when you were away, Karmaveera came as usual. I opened the magazine. I saw the picture that accompanies the story of Kashi Yatre and I could not understand anything that was written. Many times I rubbed my hands over the pages wishing they could understand what was written. But I knew it was not possible. If only I was educated enough. I waited eagerly for you to return. I felt you would come early and read for me. I even thought of going to the village and asking you to read for me. I could have asked somebody in this village but I was too embarrassed to do so. I felt very dependent and helpless. We are well-off, but what use is money when I cannot be independent?’

parts.prompt: 'Many times I rubbed my hands over the pages wishing they could understand what was written.' This action shows the grandmother's

options.text: curiosity about how the magazine was printed
helpless longing to know what the story said
anger that the episode had come late
difficulty in seeing the small print

parts.answer: (b) — she could see the picture but not read the words, and wished her hands could 'understand' for her.

parts.prompt: Why did the grandmother not ask somebody in her own village to read the story to her?
parts.answer: She was too embarrassed to do so.

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract is the opposite of 'dependent'?

options.text: helpless
educated
independent
well-off

parts.answer: (c) independent.

parts.prompt: 'We are well-off, but what use is money when I cannot be independent?' What does this question reveal about what the grandmother values? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Although her family is well-off, money could not read a page for her. She values being able to do things for herself above wealth, and sees the ability to read as the key to that independence. (1 mark: money could not help her; 1 mark: she values independence / literacy.)

questions.extract:
Then she did something unusual. She bent down and touched my feet. I was surprised and taken aback. Elders never touch the feet of youngsters. We have always touched the feet of God, elders, and teachers. We consider that as a mark of respect. It is a great tradition but today the reverse had happened. It was not correct.
She said, ‘I am touching the feet of a teacher, not my granddaughter; a teacher who taught me so well, with so much of affection that I can read any novel confidently in such a short period. Now I am independent. It is my duty to respect a teacher. Is it not written in our scriptures that a teacher should be respected, irrespective of the gender and age?’

parts.prompt: The narrator felt that 'the reverse had happened' because

options.text: an elder had touched the feet of a youngster
the grandmother had given her a gift first
she had not yet given her grandmother the novel
the ceremony was not held at the temple

parts.answer: (a) — 'Elders never touch the feet of youngsters'; the usual custom was turned the other way round.

parts.prompt: Whose feet did the grandmother say she was touching?
parts.answer: The feet of a teacher, not of her granddaughter.

parts.prompt: The phrase 'irrespective of', as used in the extract, means

options.text: because of
without regard to
in addition to
according to

parts.answer: (b) without regard to.

parts.prompt: What does the grandmother's action teach us about respect for a teacher? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: It teaches that a teacher deserves respect for the knowledge given, whatever the teacher's age or gender. The grandmother humbly honours her young granddaughter because she taught her with affection and made her independent. (1 mark: respect irrespective of age/gender; 1 mark: link to what the narrator gave her.)

questions.extract:
The mighty Himavant is ours—
there's no equal anywhere on earth.
The generous Ganga is ours—
which other river can match her grace?
The sacred Upanishads are ours—
what scriptures else to name with them?
This sunny golden land is ours—
she's peerless, let's praise her!

parts.prompt: The repetition of 'is ours' / 'are ours' in the stanza mainly expresses

options.text: a shared sense of belonging and pride in the land
the poet's claim to own land near the Himalayas
a fear that others may take these treasures away
a list of places the poet has visited

parts.answer: (a) — 'ours' speaks for all the people of the land and celebrates what they share.

parts.prompt: Which two qualities of the Ganga does the poet praise?
parts.answer: She is generous, and she has a grace no other river can match.

parts.prompt: The poet's attitude towards India in this stanza is best described as

options.text: doubtful
humorous
mournful
proud and admiring

parts.answer: (d) proud and admiring.

parts.prompt: How does the poet show, in this stanza, that India is 'peerless'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He names India's natural and spiritual treasures — the mighty Himavant, the generous Ganga, the sacred Upanishads — and after each asks, or states, that nothing anywhere can equal it, before calling it a 'sunny golden land'. (1 mark: the examples; 1 mark: the claim that none can match them.)

questions.extract:
Gallant warriors have lived here,
many a sage has sanctified this land.
The divinest music has been heard here,
and here all auspicious things are found.
Here Brahma-knowledge has taken root,
and the Buddha preached his dhamma here.
Of hoary antiquity is Bharat,
she's peerless, let's praise her!...

parts.prompt: 'Of hoary antiquity is Bharat' means that Bharat is

options.text: covered in snow and frost
very ancient
rich in hidden treasure
a recently united land

parts.answer: (b) very ancient.

parts.prompt: Name the two spiritual teachings the stanza says took root or were preached in India.
parts.answer: Brahma-knowledge, and the Buddha's dhamma.

parts.prompt: In 'many a sage has sanctified this land', the word 'sanctified' means

options.text: conquered
mapped
made famous
made holy

parts.answer: (d) made holy.

parts.prompt: How does this stanza connect India's greatness with its people and not only its land? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: It praises those who have lived here — gallant warriors for their courage, sages who made the land holy, the makers of divine music, and the Buddha's teaching — so India's greatness comes from its people's bravery, wisdom and art. (1 mark: the people named; 1 mark: what they add to India's greatness.)

questions.stem: How did the grandmother come to know the story of Kashi Yatre before she could read, and how did she respond to it? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Every Wednesday the magazine Karmaveera came and the narrator read the next episode aloud to her.
She forgot all her work and listened with the greatest concentration.
Later she could repeat the entire text by heart.
She insisted the narrator read it to her, and discussed each episode with her friends at the temple courtyard.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: How she heard the story (read aloud by the narrator each week) and how she responded to it. Any two of the value points, correctly linked.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Why did the grandmother never go to school, and how did this shape the way she raised her family? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: She lost her mother as a young girl and there was nobody to look after and guide her.
Her father was busy and married again.
In those days people did not consider education essential for girls; she was married very young.
She sometimes regretted not going to school, so she made sure her children and grandchildren studied well.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: At least two reasons she missed school, and her resolve that her children and grandchildren should study.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Why did the narrator laugh at her grandmother's decision to learn the alphabet, and how did the grandmother answer her? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: The narrator thought she was too old: sixty-two, with grey hair, wrinkled hands and spectacles.
She also pointed out how much her grandmother worked in the kitchen.
The grandmother did not take offence; she just smiled.
She replied that with determination one can overcome any obstacle for a good cause, and that 'For learning there is no age bar.'

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: The narrator's reasons for laughing and the grandmother's calm, determined reply. Any two value points, correctly linked.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: What kind of student was the grandmother, and how did the narrator know on Dassara that she had succeeded? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: She was a wonderful student who did an amazing amount of homework.
She would read, repeat, write and recite.
She had set Saraswati Puja day during Dassara as her deadline to read a novel on her own.
The narrator gave her Kashi Yatre as a gift, and she immediately read its title, the author's and the publisher's name — she had 'passed with flying colours'.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Her hard work as a student and the proof of her success on Dassara. Any two value points, correctly linked.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: What part does the novel Kashi Yatre play in the grandmother's journey to independence? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: She identified with its protagonist, an old lady who also never went to Kashi, so she longed to follow the story.
When the narrator was away, she could not read the new episode, and felt dependent and helpless.
That helplessness led to her decision to learn to read.
It was also the first book she read by herself on Dassara, so it may be seen as both the reason for and the proof of her learning.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: How the novel caused her wish to learn and how it marks her success. Any two value points; a well-argued interpretation is accepted.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: 'Bharat Our Land' is a song of praise. What does the poet choose to praise about India? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Its natural wonders: the mighty Himavant and the generous, graceful Ganga.
Its sacred texts and spiritual teachings: the Upanishads, Brahma-knowledge and the Buddha's dhamma.
Its people: gallant warriors and sages who sanctified the land, and its divine music.
Its great age ('hoary antiquity') — which is why he calls it peerless and asks us to praise it.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: At least two aspects of India the poet praises, with examples from the poem.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Your grandfather, who lives in another town, wants to learn to use a smartphone so that he can read messages and make video calls on his own. He feels embarrassed to keep asking others for help, as Krishtakka did before she learned to read. Write a letter to him, in about 100–120 words, encouraging him and suggesting how you will help.
valuePoints: Informal letter format: address, date, greeting, closing.
Understanding of his feelings — embarrassment and the wish to be independent — without mocking him.
Encouragement that there is no age bar for learning, perhaps recalling the grandmother in the story.
Practical, patient suggestions: short daily lessons, written steps, practising over calls or during a visit.
A warm, respectful tone throughout.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Empathy for his feelings, encouragement and practical ways of helping, going beyond the story.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Informal letter format; ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; warm and respectful tone and vocabulary.

questions.stem: 'For learning there is no age bar,' says the grandmother. Yet many adults believe it is too late for them to learn something new. Write an article for your school magazine, in about 100–120 words, titled 'Never Too Late to Learn', examining why adults hesitate to learn and why they should not.
valuePoints: Article format: title and writer's name; an engaging opening.
Reasons adults hesitate — embarrassment, lack of time, fear of failing, others' ridicule.
Why learning is still worthwhile — independence, confidence, keeping the mind active, new opportunities.
An example, such as Krishtakka learning to read at sixty-two, or new skills like digital literacy.
A reasoned conclusion, perhaps on how the young can support older learners.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Both sides considered — reasons for hesitation and reasons to learn — with a reasoned conclusion.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Article format (title, writer's name); introduction, body and conclusion; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; vocabulary suited to a magazine article.

questions.stem: The narrator 'childishly' laughed at her grandmother's wish to learn, and was later proved wrong. Think of a time when you doubted or made fun of someone's effort, or someone doubted yours. Write a diary entry, in about 100–120 words, reflecting on what happened, how it felt, and what you have learnt about yourself.
valuePoints: Diary format: date, first person, reflective tone.
A brief account of the situation — the effort and the doubt or mockery.
Honest feelings on either side: hurt, embarrassment, regret or determination.
Self-reflection on why the doubt arose — assumptions about age, ability or appearance.
What they have learnt and will do differently, perhaps linked to the narrator's change of heart.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: A clear situation, honest feelings and genuine self-reflection on what was learnt.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Diary format (date, first person); ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; appropriate vocabulary and personal tone.

questions.stem: Why did Arenla want her daughter to become a weaver rather than a pot maker?

options.text: She believed Sentila had no talent for working with clay.
Weaving earned more, could be done indoors in all seasons and took less time.
The village council had asked all girls to learn weaving.
The grey and red clay near the village had run out.

questions.explanation: Arenla says pot making brought her 'only a pittance', while weaving 'can be done indoors in all seasons', takes much less time for one shawl and 'the return is handsome'.

questions.stem: The village elders said that skills such as pot making did not 'belong' to any individual. What did they mean?

options.text: A potter should not sell pots for her own profit.
Only the village council may decide who learns the craft.
All the potters of the village should work in one shed.
The craft is part of the people's tradition, so experts must pass it on to anyone who wishes to learn.

questions.explanation: The elders said such skills 'catered to the needs of the people' and 'symbolised the tradition and history of the people', so experts were obliged to pass them on 'not only to their own children but also to anyone who wished to learn'.

questions.stem: 'Sentila was a quick learner and turned the clay into malleable dough.' The word 'malleable' means

options.text: able to be shaped without breaking or cracking
dry and crumbly
heavy and sticky
mixed with red and grey colour

questions.explanation: The lesson glosses 'malleable' as 'able to be put into shape without breaking or cracking' — exactly what well-pounded clay must be before it is shaped.

questions.stem: The villagers worried that 'if all pot makers followed suit, then there would be no expert potters to take their place.' Here 'followed suit' means that the other pot makers would

options.text: take the matter to the village council
give up pot making for weaving
do as Arenla seemed to be doing and not teach their children the craft
follow the traditional rules of the craft

questions.explanation: 'Followed suit' means 'did the same thing as somebody else has just done'. The villagers feared others would copy Arenla's apparent refusal to pass on the skill.

questions.stem: Which line from 'Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations' uses a sound to suggest that the worker is cheerful about the day's work?

options.text: 'The electricians humming; they get ready for work'
'The carpenters celebrating; they create anything out of wood with mathematical precision'
'Those of craftsperson, each one celebrating their craft, woven with colours and myriad hues'
'The shoemakers affirming the quality of their work'

questions.explanation: 'Humming' is a sound, and people usually hum when they are content; the other lines describe colours, precision or quality rather than a sound.

questions.extract: She said, "I shall not teach her pot making as it has brought no joy to me and only a pittance for my troubles. The riverbank, where the grey and red clay required for making pots is found, is sixteen kilometres from here. I need to climb down a sheer drop to the riverbank and my back aches from carrying the heavy load uphill all the way to the village. Pounding the stubborn clay inside bamboo cylinders to soften it, is also tedious. So many times, I've dropped the mould out of sheer exhaustion and have had to start all over again. It takes months to bring out a batch of pots after so much labour. And the reward? A few rupees.

parts.prompt: The word 'pittance' in the extract means

options.text: a heavy burden
a feeling of pity
a small amount of money
a fair wage

parts.answer: (c) a small amount of money.

parts.prompt: How far from the village is the riverbank where the clay is found?
parts.answer: Sixteen kilometres.

parts.prompt: Arenla calls the clay 'stubborn' because it

options.text: is found only at the bottom of a sheer drop
is hard and has to be pounded for a long time to soften
changes colour when it is fired
cracks as soon as it dries in the sun

parts.answer: (b) — it resists softening, which makes pounding it 'tedious'.

parts.prompt: What hardships of pot making does Arenla describe, and what do her words reveal about how she feels? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: She climbs down a sheer drop and carries heavy clay sixteen kilometres uphill, pounds stubborn clay and starts again when exhaustion makes her drop the mould — all for a few rupees. She feels worn out and unrewarded. (1 mark: any two hardships; 1 mark: her feelings.)

questions.extract: On her way back, Onula noticed that the door to the work shed was slightly ajar. Out of curiosity, she stepped inside and abruptly stopped in her tracks; two neat rows of newly-made pots stood side by side. She could find nothing to tell one batch from the other. She was sure that it was not the handiwork of one person alone. Onula stood there for a long time as if trying to absorb a new phenomenon. Slowly she walked away from this place of wonder, as she considered it to be, because she believed that she had just witnessed a profound revelation in the two batches of still moist pots, standing side by side in perfect symmetry inside the shed.

parts.prompt: Onula 'could find nothing to tell one batch from the other'. This suggests that

options.text: Arenla had made both batches herself
the pots had all been made from the same lump of clay
Onula did not know much about pot making
Sentila's pots were now as skilfully made as her mother's

parts.answer: (d) — Onula was sure two people had made them, yet the daughter's work matched the mother's.

parts.prompt: How did Onula regard the work shed as she walked away?
parts.answer: As a place of wonder.

parts.prompt: A 'profound revelation', as used in the extract, is

options.text: a powerful moment of realisation
a secret that must be hidden
a sad and frightening event
a story told by the villagers

parts.answer: (a) a powerful moment of realisation.

parts.prompt: What 'revelation' might Onula have witnessed in the two rows of pots? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: She may have realised that Arenla's skill had passed fully to Sentila on the very day Arenla died — the craft handed down from one generation to the next. A new pot maker had been born. (1 mark: the skill passed from mother to daughter; 1 mark: its significance. Accept well-argued alternatives.)

questions.poem: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
questions.extract:
I hear Bharat celebrating, the varied vocations I hear;
Those of craftsperson, each one celebrating their craft, woven with colours and myriad hues.
The artisans with lutes, each hailing varied emotions and celebrating dreams, echoing in the streets.
The carpenters celebrating; they create anything out of wood with mathematical precision,
The electricians humming; they get ready for work, work with cables and wires to brighten our lives,

parts.prompt: In 'woven with colours and myriad hues', the word 'myriad' means

options.text: faded
countless
costly
matching

parts.answer: (b) countless.

parts.prompt: What quality does the poet admire in the work of carpenters?
parts.answer: Their mathematical precision — they can create anything out of wood.

parts.prompt: The electricians work 'to brighten our lives'. The phrase suggests that they

options.text: only fit lights in homes
cheer people up by singing
bring light and also make daily life better
work mostly at night

parts.answer: (c) — literally they bring light; figuratively they make our lives better.

parts.prompt: What idea does the opening line, 'I hear Bharat celebrating, the varied vocations I hear', introduce? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: It presents a whole country joyfully celebrating the many different kinds of work its people do. The speaker 'hears' this celebration, suggesting every vocation has its own voice, and all deserve to be honoured. (1 mark: celebration of varied vocations across the nation; 1 mark: respect / every vocation has a voice.)

questions.poem: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations
questions.extract:
The boatmen gathering their nets from the shore, sailing, and singing while at work, return to tell the tales of life at sea,
The shoemakers affirming the quality of their work, for the feet that walk, dance, run, jump, return home.
The delicious singing of the cook, or the rhythm of designer, mason, each celebrating what belongs to them and to none else,
The voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity.
I hear Bharat celebrating, the varied voices I hear!

parts.prompt: The boatmen 'return to tell the tales of life at sea'. This suggests that their work

options.text: is so dangerous that few return
is done only for entertainment
keeps them away from their families for years
gives them experiences and stories worth sharing

parts.answer: (d) gives them experiences and stories worth sharing.

parts.prompt: Which two workers are mentioned along with the cook in these lines?
parts.answer: The designer and the mason.

parts.prompt: 'each celebrating what belongs to them and to none else' suggests that each worker's skill is

options.text: shared equally with every other worker
less important than the cook's
distinct and their own
kept secret from their children

parts.answer: (c) distinct and their own.

parts.prompt: Explain the line 'The voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity.' Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: A person's work expresses who they are: the boatman's songs, the shoemaker's pride in quality and the cook's singing all speak for the worker. So their work is not just a job but part of their identity, and deserves respect. (1 mark: work expresses identity; 1 mark: example or the dignity it implies.)

questions.stem: Describe what Sentila saw when she secretly watched the expert potters at work. Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: The clay was mixed with water and pounded.
The potters carefully pushed the left hand into the softened lump and deftly rotated it, shaping it with a spatula in the right hand.
The regular 'tap, tap' of the spatula was music to her ears as a pot emerged from a shapeless lump.
The pots were dried in the sun, loaded on to a kiln on hay and dried bamboo, and fired, with the fire tended carefully.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: At least two stages of the process she watched, described accurately in order.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Why was Mesoba summoned by the village council, and how did he respond? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Sentila's visits to the potters had become village gossip; people wondered why Arenla would not teach her.
The villagers feared there would be no expert potters left if others did the same.
Mesoba humbly said Arenla had never refused; they only wanted Sentila to grow stronger after her illness.
He promised the elders they would soon see Sentila making the best pots in the village.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: The reason he was summoned and his humble, reassuring reply. Any two value points, correctly linked.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: How did Onula help Sentila when she saw her struggling with the clay in the dormitory? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: She noticed that Sentila was too tense, so the clay would not take the right shape.
She comforted her — 'Don't worry, little one' — and showed her how to make a perfect pot.
Sentila tried again with new confidence and made a beautiful pot.
Onula pointed out that the mouth was wrong and advised her to watch her mother shaping the mouth.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: What Onula noticed and at least two ways she helped, including her advice to watch Arenla.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: On the last sunny day, Arenla left Sentila alone in the shed, saying she had a headache and a backache. Why might this have helped Sentila finally succeed? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Earlier, Arenla had sat watching, and Sentila had failed and hung her head in shame; Onula had noticed she was too tense.
Alone, and asked to make as many pots as she could, she may have worked without the pressure of being watched.
She had carefully observed her mother's hands, and now she worked with the same speed and dexterity.
Whether Arenla meant it as a chance or was truly unwell is open — the story shows she was in fact ill; accept a reasoned view.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: A reasoned explanation linking working alone to her earlier tension and her careful observation. Well-argued interpretations accepted.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: As her mother's body was carried away, Sentila cried, 'Mother, I did not wish it to happen this way; it simply came to me. Please forgive me.' What might she have meant? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: 'It' may refer to the skill of pot making, which came to her that very day, when she made one pot short of her mother's tally.
She had long dreamed of being a pot maker, and it happened at the moment she lost her mother.
She may have felt guilty, as if her success had come at her mother's cost.
She asks forgiveness out of grief, though she had done nothing wrong.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: A sensitive interpretation linking 'it' to the skill that came to her and her grief or guilt. Well-argued alternatives accepted.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: How does the poem 'Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations' show that every kind of work has dignity? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: It celebrates many different workers — craftspersons, artisans, carpenters, electricians, boatmen, shoemakers, cooks, designers and masons — without ranking them.
It shows what each gives others: electricians brighten our lives; shoemakers serve the feet that walk, dance and run.
Each celebrates what belongs to them, and 'The voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity.'
The whole of Bharat is heard celebrating these vocations.

rubric.label: Content

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about hand fans is supported by 'Winds of Change'?

options.text: Gujarat is known for pankhas made from the spongy centre of the sola.
Zardozi hand fans with gold threadwork come from Kutch.
The painted cardboard hand fans of Bihar are offered to gods.
Kutch is known for hand-stitched leather fans decorated with thread and wool at the seams.

questions.explanation: The chapter says 'Kutch is recognised for its hand-stitched leather hand fans decorated with thread and wool at its seams.' Sola fans are from Bengal, and the zardozi and painted hand fans are described under Rajasthan.

questions.stem: Why, according to the chapter, does the culture of pankhas run 'the risk of slowly losing its presence among Indians'?

Because the materials used to make them are no longer found.
Because temples and royal courts have banned their use.
Because artisans refuse to make versions for sale.

Written records of trade routes
Buddhist wall paintings at Ajanta dating back to the 2nd century CE
Brass fans found inside ancient temples

questions.stem: 'Take responsibility' is called a collocation. This is because

options.text: the two words are joined by 'and' in a fixed order
the words form a conventional combination that is naturally used together
the two words have opposite meanings
the shorter word always comes first

thin and thick

questions.extract: In modern times, the use of pankhas has been restricted to decorative purposes, and they have become traditional craft items in India. The structure of each fan reflects the cultural core of the region that crafts it. For instance, the appliqué hand fan of Rajasthan is an antique pankha made of pieces of fabric in different shapes and patterns sewn onto another cloth with the use of ornamental needlework. Furthermore, the zardozi hand fan of Rajasthan differs in its use of glittering ornate and encrusted gold threadwork. In Rajasthan, temple hand fans are popular too. These are made by engraving brass and have a long handle. The painted hand fan, a cardboard pankha featuring various images, is usually offered to gods.

parts.prompt: 'The structure of each fan reflects the cultural core of the region that crafts it.' This means that

options.text: every region makes exactly the same kind of fan
a fan's design and materials show the culture of the place where it is made
fans are made only in the centre of each region
the largest fans come from the richest regions

parts.answer: (b) — the chapter then gives Rajasthan's fans as examples.

parts.prompt: How are the temple hand fans of Rajasthan made?
parts.answer: By engraving brass; they have a long handle.

parts.prompt: The word 'ornate' in 'glittering ornate and encrusted gold threadwork' means

options.text: richly decorated
plain and simple
old and worn
light in weight

parts.answer: (a) richly decorated.

parts.prompt: How is the appliqué hand fan of Rajasthan different from its zardozi hand fan? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The appliqué fan is made of pieces of fabric in different shapes and patterns sewn onto another cloth with ornamental needlework. The zardozi fan instead uses glittering, ornate, encrusted gold threadwork. (1 mark: appliqué; 1 mark: zardozi.)

questions.extract: One of the first steps to preserve the essence of the craft is by celebrating pankhas, and appreciating the culture, stories, and artistry that this handicraft invokes. This allows contemporary pankha makers to demonstrate their craft and regain its popularity. It also helps provide them with a commercial platform to create a sustainable livelihood. parts.prompt: A 'sustainable livelihood' is

options.text: a hobby done in free time
a job given by the government
a way of earning a living that can continue over time
a one-time prize for good work

parts.prompt: Name one initiative the extract suggests for spreading awareness about the craft.
parts.answer: Pankha-making workshops, within and outside handicraft exhibitions.

parts.prompt: The word 'contemporary' in 'contemporary pankha makers' means

options.text: temporary
highly skilled
belonging to royal families
of the present time

parts.answer: (d) of the present time.

parts.prompt: How can celebrating pankhas help both the craft and its makers? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Celebrating pankhas lets today's makers show their craft and helps it regain popularity, which preserves its essence. It also gives them a commercial platform, so they can earn a sustainable livelihood from it. (1 mark: benefit to the craft; 1 mark: benefit to the makers.)

questions.extract:
Palette of earth, rich and deep,
Where dreams of gardeners seep.
Brushstrokes of seeds, planted true,
Awaiting spring's vibrant hue.

parts.prompt: The earth is called a 'palette' because, like a painter's palette, it

options.text: holds the rich material from which a garden's colours will come
is thin and oval in shape
is washed clean after every season
belongs only to trained artists

parts.answer: (a) — a palette holds the colours a painter uses; the rich, deep earth holds what the gardener will 'paint' with.

parts.prompt: What are the seeds compared to in the stanza?
parts.answer: Brushstrokes.

parts.prompt: 'Awaiting spring's vibrant hue' suggests that the seeds

options.text: have been planted in the wrong season
will be painted by the gardener in spring
will grow into brightly coloured plants and flowers in spring
are already blooming in many colours

parts.answer: (c) — the colour will come when they grow in spring.

parts.prompt: How does this stanza present gardeners as artists? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Through metaphor: the earth is their palette and the seeds, planted carefully, are their brushstrokes. Their dreams seep into the soil, and like painters they wait for the colours of spring to complete the picture. (1 mark: the painting metaphors; 1 mark: how this makes the gardener an artist.)

questions.extract:
Each plot, a canvas wide,
Where art and life coincide.
In the hands of those who till,
Gardens become paintings still.

parts.prompt: 'Those who till' are

options.text: painters who buy canvases
gardeners who work the soil
visitors who admire gardens
shopkeepers who count their money

parts.answer: (b) gardeners who work the soil.

parts.prompt: What is each plot of land compared to?
parts.answer: A wide canvas.

parts.prompt: Which pair of words rhymes in this stanza?

options.text: plot / art
canvas / gardens
life / hands
till / still

parts.answer: (d) till / still (and wide / coincide).

parts.prompt: What does the poet mean by 'Where art and life coincide'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: In a garden, art and living things meet: the plants are alive and growing, yet the gardener arranges them with an artist's eye, so the plot becomes a living painting. Creativity and nature happen in the same place. (1 mark: living growth; 1 mark: artistic creation in the same place.)

questions.stem: At the start of the story, Ravi's mother wishes someone would invent 'Vitamin-M' for old people. By the end, Grandpa says his daughter needs it. What makes this ironic?

Grandpa had forgotten the way home from the barber shop.
Ravi's father had forgotten to buy the Tamil newspaper.

questions.stem: On the bus, Ravi realised the man in the yellow cap was not Grandpa. Which detail had made him sure, until then, that it was Grandpa's cap?

options.text: It was bright yellow, which only Grandpa wore.
It had Grandpa's name written inside it.
It had a coffee-stain on its rim just like Grandpa's.
It was being worn with a mahogany walking stick.

questions.explanation: The text says the cap 'had a coffee-strain on its rim just like Grandpa's'. The stranger explained that a kind old gentleman in the barber shop had insisted he take it because it was a hot day.

questions.stem: Grandpa gives Ravi The Best Detective Stories and says he can learn 'how to avoid getting fooled when one is trailing a suspect'. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.text: Grandpa had forgotten what Ravi liked to read.
Grandpa wanted Ravi to become a detective when he grew up.
Grandpa was angry that Ravi had left him alone at home.
Grandpa probably knew Ravi had followed him and had fooled him on purpose.

questions.explanation: The remark matches exactly what happened to Ravi on the bus, where he trailed the wrong man. Together with 'the twinkle in Grandpa's eye', it suggests Grandpa knew all along — not forgetfulness but mischief.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Ravi took position behind a big banyan tree to watch him', the word 'behind' is a preposition. What relationship does it show?

the time at which Ravi watched Grandpa
the manner in which Ravi moved
the reason Ravi was hiding

questions.stem: In 'I Cannot Remember My Mother', the poet says the scent of the shiuli flowers 'comes to me as the scent of my mother'. The flowers here work as a symbol. What do they stand for?

options.text: the beauty of the autumn season
the poet's wish to visit the temple
the presence of the mother the poet cannot remember
the poet's sorrow at the end of summer

questions.explanation: Symbolism, as the chapter explains, is a tangible object representing something beyond its literal meaning. The poet cannot remember his mother, but the smell of the shiuli flowers brings her presence to him.

questions.extract:

uncomfortable that she spoke to Grandpa as if he were a child
angry that she was leaving for work
confused about which medicines to give

fear
sympathy
indifference

parts.prompt: Ravi promises that 'Grandpa'll be fine at home with me'. Why does this promise turn out to be hard to keep? Answer in 30–40 words.

parts.prompt: Ravi's mother 'flushed' because she

was surprised to receive a gift herself
felt unwell after a long day at the office
realised she had forgotten her father's birthday

counted carefully
shouted angrily
whispered secretly

smell
sight
touch

a refrain

to show that Shruti is shouting at her friends
to tell the actors how to tune their instruments
to mark the end of the act

a father should never interfere in his child's life

questions.stem: Khetaram delivers even when the temperature has crossed 50 degrees celsius, but it 'is recorded as 49.9 degrees celsius'. What does this detail reveal?

options.text: The thermometers in the desert are not accurate.
Recording 50 degrees would mean a state holiday, so the work goes on in extreme heat.
Khetaram prefers to deliver mail only on the hottest days.
The temperature in the Thar never actually reaches 50 degrees.

questions.explanation: The text says the temperature 'is recorded as 49.9 degrees celsius, since 50 degrees celsius would mean a state holiday'. Khetaram's body tells him it is hotter, yet he keeps delivering — a sign of how harsh his working conditions are.

questions.stem: Khetaram says, "When I finish, there is a sand dune at my feet every evening." What is the effect of this exaggeration?

options.text: It shows that he builds sand dunes as a hobby after work.
It suggests that he is careless about keeping himself clean.
It stresses how much sand the desert winds cover him with during the day.
It proves that the post office is built on a sand dune.

questions.explanation: This is hyperbole. The sandstorms 'turn him into a walking sandman', and since water is too precious for washing he can only wipe his body — the 'sand dune at my feet' exaggerates how much sand he carries home.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences from the chapter is in the passive voice?

options.text: He delivers even on days when his body sends blazing signals.
People are kind to me; the BSF always gives me a lift.
Khetaram says his spine is strong.
The mail was dropped in the post box.

questions.explanation: In 'The mail was dropped in the post box' the subject (the mail) receives the action, and the verb is 'was' + past participle. In the other sentences the subject does the action.

questions.stem: 'In the village, a piece of jaggery is all that can be offered when he brings news of a birth or weddings.' What does this line most suggest about the villagers?

options.text: They have little to give, yet they value the news he carries and want to thank him.
They expect Khetaram to pay for good news.
They are unhappy with the service of the post office.
They offer jaggery only to officials of the BSF.

questions.explanation: 'All that can be offered' shows how little the villagers of this arid, famine-hit land have; offering it anyway shows gratitude and the warmth with which Khetaram, 'a warmly received man', is treated.

questions.stem: In 'Words', the poet says words, 'like summer birds, depart, / And leave but empty air.' What does this simile convey?

options.text: Words are as colourful and cheerful as birds in summer.
Words pass away quickly and leave nothing lasting behind.
Words travel long distances like migrating birds.
Words can only be heard clearly in summer.

questions.explanation: Summer birds fly away and leave 'but empty air'. In the same way, words that do not come from the heart are soon gone and leave nothing behind — which is why they cannot 'satisfy the heart'.

questions.extract: Often, the impression of his footprints reveals the weight of his mailbag. Regulations stipulate that his load cannot exceed 28 kilos. But in the summers, when the sands sizzle under his mojri-clad feet, Khetaram says, "Even a single delivery is tiring, as I have to cover 20 km for it." He delivers even on days when his body sends blazing signals that the temperature has crossed 50 degrees celsius, but is recorded as 49.9 degrees celsius, since 50 degrees celsius would mean a state holiday. Sometimes severe heat forces him to postpone deliveries till after sundown.

parts.prompt: The word 'stipulate', as used in the extract, means

options.text: forbid
suggest
specify
increase

parts.answer: (c) specify — the regulations lay down that his load cannot exceed 28 kilos.

parts.prompt: According to the extract, what reveals the weight of Khetaram's mailbag?
parts.answer: The impression of his footprints (in the sand).

parts.prompt: Which poetic device is used in 'the sands sizzle'?

options.text: alliteration
simile
rhetorical question
antithesis

parts.answer: (a) alliteration — the repeated 's' sound in 'sands sizzle' (it also suggests the sound of the heat).

parts.prompt: What do the details in the extract tell us about the hardships of Khetaram's work? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He walks 20 km for a single delivery carrying up to 28 kilos, on sand that sizzles in summer. He works even above 50 degrees, and severe heat sometimes forces him to deliver after sundown. (1 mark: distance and load; 1 mark: the extreme heat.)

questions.extract: When writing about the social significance of the money order in his book, Story of the Indian Post Office, Mulk Raj Anand says, "In no other country a person in remote villages is so dependent on the post office for transmission of small sums of money...It reflects the absolute confidence which most Indians place in the post office." In fact, a few years ago, a scheme to scrap the GDS and transfer the job to patwaris (village record keepers) was proposed and summarily rejected. "We knew they would not be able to do the job," says Budh Singh, a village elder.

parts.prompt: The word 'transmission', as used in the extract, means

options.text: saving
counting
borrowing
sending

parts.answer: (d) sending — the post office sends small sums of money to people in remote villages.

parts.prompt: To whom did the proposed scheme want to transfer the job of the GDS?
parts.answer: To patwaris (village record keepers).

parts.prompt: The clause 'a scheme ... was proposed and summarily rejected' is in the passive voice because

options.text: the subject, 'a scheme', receives the action
it describes something that happened in the past
it contains two verbs joined by 'and'
the subject, 'a scheme', performs the action

parts.answer: (a) — the scheme did not propose or reject anything; it was proposed and rejected by others (was + past participle).

parts.prompt: What do Mulk Raj Anand's words and Budh Singh's remark together show about the place of the post office in village life? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Villagers depend on the post office to receive money and place 'absolute confidence' in it. They trusted the GDS so much that they rejected handing the job to patwaris, believing no one else could do it. (1 mark: dependence and confidence; 1 mark: trust shown by the rejection.)

questions.extract:
A little said, and truly said,
Can deeper joy impart
Than hosts of words, which reach the head,
But never touch the heart.

The voice that wins its sunny way,
A lonely home to cheer,
Hath oft the fewest words to say;
But, oh! those few, how dear!

parts.prompt: The word 'impart', as used in the extract, means

options.text: hide
give
divide
demand

parts.answer: (b) give — a few true words can give deeper joy.

parts.prompt: Which phrase in the extract means 'a very large number of words'?
parts.answer: 'hosts of words'.

parts.prompt: 'Hath oft the fewest words to say' means that such a voice

options.text: never speaks at all
always talks the most
often says very little
only speaks to lonely people

parts.answer: (c) often says very little — 'hath' is 'has' and 'oft' is 'often'.

parts.prompt: What contrast does the poet draw between 'a little said, and truly said' and 'hosts of words'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: A few sincere words bring deeper joy and cheer even a lonely home, so they are dear. Many words may reach the mind but 'never touch the heart'. (1 mark: what few true words do; 1 mark: the limit of many words.)

questions.extract:
If words could satisfy the chest,
The world might hold a feast;
But words, when summoned to the test,
Oft satisfy the least!

Like plants that make a gaudy show,
All blossom to the root;
But whose poor nature cannot grow,
One particle of fruit!

parts.prompt: Which poetic device is used in 'The world might hold a feast'?

options.text: personification only
alliteration
simile
hyperbole

parts.answer: (d) hyperbole — the whole world celebrating with a feast is an exaggeration of how satisfying words would be if they could fill the heart.

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract means 'showy and bright in a way that lacks real worth'?
parts.answer: 'gaudy'.

parts.prompt: The rhyme scheme of the first stanza of the extract is

options.text: abab
aabb
abba
abcb

parts.answer: (a) abab — chest/test and feast/least.

parts.prompt: Why does the poet compare words to 'plants that make a gaudy show'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Such plants are covered in blossom but cannot grow 'one particle of fruit'. Likewise, many words look impressive but produce nothing of real value; when put to the test they satisfy least. (1 mark: the plant image; 1 mark: its application to words.)

questions.stem: According to the mother, what should a person do after feeling the conviction that it is imperative to realise a dream, and before plunging into it?

options.text: Count the cost in years of effort, financial investments and sacrifice.
Ask others to form a support network first.
Wait until life changes the dream.
Trade the dream for security.

questions.explanation: The letter gives the order: passion, then conviction, then 'Count the cost in years of effort, financial investments and sacrifice. Then if it is still burning in your blood ... plunge.'

questions.stem: The mother mentions that publishing this book is a dream she has chased in the last ten years, though it 'was not the dream I had in my youth'. What point does this example support?

options.text: Dreams of youth are the only ones worth pursuing.
A dream should be abandoned once it takes ten years.
A dream that comes later in life is no less than the original dream of younger days.
Writing books is easier than following other dreams.

questions.explanation: She says life itself may change a person's dreams and 'these hopes and aspirations are no less than the original dream of younger days'. Her own book, a changed dream, is the proof.

questions.stem: 'Dreamscape' combines 'dream' with '-scape', which means 'a view or scene of'. In the letter, 'the people who are participants in your dreamscape' are

options.text: people who appear in one's dreams at night
people who paint scenes of nature
people who discourage a dreamer
people who become part of the world of one's dream as it is pursued

questions.explanation: The glossary gives 'dreamscape: a world of dreams'. As a dream takes longer to realise, more people take part in that world — helpers, supporters and others involved in the pursuit.

questions.stem: "No, I am not going to put a wet blanket on your dreams". Through this idiom the mother assures Ming that she

options.text: will pay for all the costs of the dream
does not want to discourage her or spoil her enthusiasm
wants her to forget her dreams completely
will protect her from every difficulty

questions.explanation: A 'wet blanket' is someone who spoils others' enthusiasm. The mother does not want to discourage Ming, even while asking her to consider the years a dream needs.

questions.stem: 'There is such ease in comfort / To maintain the status quo, / But this isn't what we are made for'. What does the speaker suggest?

options.text: Change should be avoided because it is uncomfortable.
Comfort is the reward for hard work.
Keeping things as they are is easy, but it stops us from growing.
People are made to stay in familiar places.

questions.explanation: The poem admits the ease of keeping the status quo (the existing state of affairs) but says 'this isn't what we are made for / This isn't how we grow' — growth needs change.

questions.extract:
By all means follow that dream.
Great men and women become great because they have a dream and they pursue it till it comes true. What differentiates greatness from the ordinary is how much effort and sacrifice people invest to realise their dream. Do you know that to reach world-class standard in any field, one has to be singularly and intensively pursuing the subject for at least ten years?

parts.prompt: The word 'singularly', as used in the extract, means

options.text: strangely
exclusively
occasionally
alone

parts.answer: (b) exclusively — focusing on that one subject.

parts.prompt: According to the extract, what differentiates greatness from the ordinary?
parts.answer: How much effort and sacrifice people invest to realise their dream.

parts.prompt: The opening line 'By all means follow that dream' shows that the mother

options.text: is unsure about Ming's dream
is ordering Ming to change her dream
is warning Ming against dreaming
wholeheartedly encourages Ming

parts.answer: (d) — 'by all means' expresses full approval and encouragement.

parts.prompt: Why do you think the mother asks Ming whether she knows about the 'at least ten years' needed to reach world-class standard? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The question makes Ming think about how long and focused the effort must be. It encourages her while preparing her for years of intense work, so she does not expect quick success. (1 mark: shows the time and focus needed; 1 mark: purpose — realistic encouragement.)

questions.extract:
When you watch the Academy Awards for best actors and actresses and films, the winner always thanks a host of people that formed his/her support network. So, you see that for one winner, there is a group of people who stood by him/her.
It is good to be able to fulfil your dreams but for a lot of people, dreams remain dreams. Although everyone at one time or other has wistfully said to oneself, "I wish I could be this or the other," they have never got beyond just wishful thinking. They could have preferred to trade their dream for security. Perhaps circumstances changed their lives.

parts.prompt: The word 'wistfully', as used in the extract, means

options.text: angrily
cleverly
longingly
proudly

parts.answer: (c) longingly.

parts.prompt: According to the extract, what might some people have traded their dream for?
parts.answer: Security.

parts.prompt: 'They have never got beyond just wishful thinking' means that they

options.text: hoped for something but did nothing to make it happen
worked hard but failed
achieved more than they had wished
thought carefully before choosing a dream

parts.answer: (a) — wishful thinking is hoping for something without acting to achieve it.

parts.prompt: What point does the mother make through the example of the Academy Awards? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Every winner thanks many people who formed their support network, so success is never achieved alone: behind one winner stands a group of people. A dreamer needs, and should value, such support. (1 mark: winners thank a support network; 1 mark: the lesson for a dreamer.)

questions.extract:
Step up to the challenge
There is no crowd to see,
It's just you and the future
And where you want to be.
Will it pull you forward
Or push you back in fear?
Difficult are choices
When the future is getting near.

parts.prompt: In 'Difficult are choices', the usual word order ('Choices are difficult') is reversed. This device is called

options.text: simile
alliteration
onomatopoeia
inversion

parts.answer: (d) inversion — it places emphasis on 'Difficult'.

parts.prompt: Quote the rhetorical question from the extract.
parts.answer: 'Will it pull you forward / Or push you back in fear?'

parts.prompt: The phrase 'Step up to' in the first line means

options.text: run away from
come forward to face
climb over
watch from a distance

parts.answer: (b) come forward to face (the challenge).

parts.prompt: Why, according to the extract, do choices become difficult 'when the future is getting near'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: As the moment of decision comes close, a person faces it alone ('just you and the future') and is torn between moving forward and being pushed back by fear, which makes choosing hard. (1 mark: facing it alone/near; 1 mark: the pull between hope and fear.)

questions.extract:
There is such ease in comfort
To maintain the status quo,
But this isn't what we are made for
This isn't how we grow.
The first step is the hardest
There is no turning back,
You just need to believe in yourself
For your future to be on track.

parts.prompt: 'Status quo', as used in the extract, means

options.text: the existing state of things
a sudden change
a high position in society
a plan for the future

parts.answer: (a) the existing state of things — keeping things the same.

parts.prompt: Which line in the extract tells us that once the first step is taken, one cannot retreat?
parts.answer: 'There is no turning back'.

parts.prompt: How does the poem end?

options.text: With a warning that the future is uncertain
With advice to seek comfort after a hard step
With the assurance that self-belief keeps one's future on track
With a question about whether to take the first step

parts.answer: (c) — 'You just need to believe in yourself / For your future to be on track.'

parts.prompt: Why does the poet say that comfort 'isn't how we grow'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Staying in comfort keeps things unchanged, and nothing unchanged can grow. Growth needs the hard first step into challenge; though difficult, it moves us forward, supported by belief in ourselves. (1 mark: comfort means no change; 1 mark: growth needs the difficult step.)

questions.stem: What steps does the mother describe for pursuing a dream? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: It starts with a passion for a particular interest.
Then comes the conviction that it is imperative to realise it.
Count the cost in years of effort, financial investments and sacrifice.
If it is still burning in your blood and you are ready to commit, plunge.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: The steps in the right order — passion, conviction, counting the cost, committing and plunging. At least three steps.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: According to the mother, why do dreams remain only dreams for many people? Answer in 40–50 words.
